## 1 Samuel 27 — Overview

Most traditional commentators agree this is one of the darkest chapters in David's life. Precept Austin notes that God's name is never mentioned in the chapter, David never inquires of the Lord, and most writers agree he wrote no psalms during this 16-month period: "He went from a physical wilderness to a spiritual wilderness."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-27-commentary

Ellicott calls it "the saddest portion of David's career" — he had adopted the very course his bitterest foes would have wished, living as a vassal of the Philistine king whose champion he once slew.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-27.html

David Guzik (Enduring Word / Pentecostal-charismatic) calls it "one of the saddest chapters in David's life, where discouragement and despair — not Saul's pursuit — drive him to abandon Israel."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-27/

---

### v. 1 — David's discouraged decision

**Traditional reading:** David "said in his heart" (literally "spoke to his heart") that Saul would eventually kill him. All major commentators see this as a failure of faith, not a rational military decision.

- **Gill (Baptist/Reformed):** "This was a strange fit of unbelief he was sunk into, and very unaccountable and unreasonable it was, had he but considered his being anointed king by the Lord, the promise of God to him, which could not fail, and the providence of God that watched over him from time to time." Gill also notes the irony: David had earlier cursed those who would drive him into an idolatrous land (1 Sam 26:19), yet now he goes willingly.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** "In this determination of the son of Jesse we never hear of prayer, or of consultation with prophet or with priest. A dull despair seems to have at this time deprived David at once of faith and hope."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Constable (Evangelical/Dispensational):** Three reasons indicate David should not have done this: (1) He consulted only himself, whereas previously he inquired of God (1 Sam 23:2, 4). (2) He said he would die, yet God had promised him the throne through Samuel, Jonathan, Saul himself, and Abigail. (3) God's name never appears in the chapter. Yet Constable adds this was "only a weakness in trust, not disobedience to the revealed will of God."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Precept Austin (Evangelical):** Notes the proliferation of personal pronouns with no mention of Yahweh. "David was walking by sight (horizontal vision), not by faith (vertical vision)." Quotes Spurgeon: "He certainly had no ground for thinking that God's anointing him by Samuel was intended to be left as an empty unmeaning act." Also quotes Alan Redpath: "He traded the smile of God for the grin of the devil."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-27-commentary

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** "What we say in our heart has a tremendous power to shape our thinking, our actions, even our whole destiny… Discouragement and despair are more dangerous enemies than any earthly pursuer; they drove David to do something Saul could never have forced him to do."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-27/

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** Calls David's resolution "in every respect, wrong": (1) It removed him from where the divine oracle told him to stay (1 Sam 22:5). (2) It drove him into the very idolatrous land for which he had cursed his enemies (1 Sam 26:19). (3) It withdrew his counsel and aid from God's people. Yet Providence overruled it.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_samuel/27.htm

---

### vv. 2–3 — David crosses to Gath with his household

- **Gill:** Notes that David's circumstances were vastly different from his earlier visit to Gath (1 Sam 21:10–15): then he was alone and feigned madness; now he comes openly with 600 men and their families. The families served as pledges of fidelity to Achish.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Ellicott:** Achish is "the same, we believe, as that Achish to whom David fled before" (1 Sam 21:11) and identical with Achish son of Maachah (1 Kings 2:39), which would require a reign of about 50 years — "quite possible." He adds that David later permitted Achish to remain as a tributary king in Gath, repaying the old debt of kindness.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Enduring Word:** Emphasises that David's defection touched not only the 600 fighting men but all their families, including Ahinoam and Abigail. David led others into compromise. Also notes Achish received David now (unlike in ch. 21) because (a) they now share the same enemy, Saul, and (b) David brings 600 mercenaries.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-27/

---

### v. 4 — Saul stops pursuing David

- **Gill:** Saul "very probably had his spies out to watch his motions." Once David was in enemy territory, Saul "laid aside all thoughts of seeking after him."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Matthew Henry:** "We may blush to think that the word of a Philistine should go further than the word of an Israelite, and that the city of Gath should be a place of refuge for a good man, when the cities of Israel refuse him a safe abode."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/27.htm

- **Precept Austin:** David's immediate goal was achieved — Saul stopped pursuing. But the text's silence about God underscores the spiritual cost: David escaped Saul only to enter a far more dangerous spiritual compromise.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-27-commentary

---

### vv. 5–6 — David requests Ziklag; Achish grants it

- **Gill:** David asked for a place "in some town in the country" to avoid the envy of Achish's courtiers, to preserve his people from idolatrous temptations in the capital, and to have freedom to raid Israel's enemies without Achish knowing. Ziklag had originally been assigned to Judah (Josh 15:31) then Simeon (Josh 19:5), but had been held by the Philistines until now. It "returned to its right owners" and became annexed to the crown lands of Judah's kings permanently.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Ellicott:** The real reason for the request was that David could conduct his forays "apart from the supervision of his Philistine friends." Achish expected David to harry southern Judah; David intended instead to harry the nomad foes of Israel.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** "David did not feel at home… At Ziklag he would be less under restraint, and his real sentiments less likely to be discovered." It notes the contradiction between David's apparent and real character, and that "no outward advantages that good men may gain by their alliance with the ungodly can afford adequate compensation for the insincerity, distraction, restlessness, and vexation of soul which it involves."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/27.htm

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** Calls the request "a prudent arrangement": it prevented jealous suspicion, placed his followers beyond contamination by the idolatries of the capital, and gave opportunity for reprisals against freebooting tribes on the Israel-Philistine border.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_samuel/27.htm

- **Constable:** Achish treated David as "a vassal ruler" and gave Ziklag as "a fiefdom." The town stood about 27 miles south-southwest of Gerar. From Ziklag, "David could come and go without constant observation by the Philistines who lived mainly to the north."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-27.html

---

### v. 7 — Duration: a full year and four months

- **Ellicott:** The Hebrew phrase is *yamim* — literally "days" — a collective term used in Lev 25:29 and 1 Sam 1:3 to signify a full year. These were "among the darkest days of David's life." He was like "an Italian condottiere or captain of free lances of the Middle Ages," taking service with the very city whose champion he had slain.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Gill:** Notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate read only "four months." The Jewish chronology (*Seder Olam Rabba*) records that Samuel died four months before Saul, and David left Philistia when Saul died, so the period was indeed four months. But the traditional rendering is "a year [lit. 'days'] and four months."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Enduring Word / Precept Austin:** Both stress that there is no record of David writing any psalms during these 16 months — "the sweet singer was mute."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-27/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-27-commentary

---

### vv. 8–9 — David's raids on the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites

**Traditional reading:** This is the most ethically difficult part of the chapter. Commentators take different approaches to whether David's actions were justified or sinful.

- **Gill (justifying):** These were old Canaanite inhabitants whom Israel had been commanded to destroy (Deut 7:2; Deut 3:14; Josh 13:2; Josh 16:3) plus Amalekites (sworn enemies under the ban). "David had a just right to invade them… which may be observed to remove the charge of cruelty that might be brought against David on this account."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Ellicott (critical):** "These acts of ferocious barbarity are simply without excuse." Though Israel had been commanded in a few instances to wage wars of extermination, "David had no such charge." Ellicott asks: "Was it not these acts of ruthless cruelty which left on this king's hands the stain of blood which rendered them unfit in after days to build the House of the Lord?" (citing 1 Chron 28:3).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Enduring Word (severely critical):** The Hebrew verb for "raided" (*pashat*) comes from the idea of stripping the dead for loot. "David was nothing more than an armed robber and murderer… He now fought wars for profit instead of for God's honor." Guzik sees here the roots of the pattern (covering sin with murder) that would later bear bitter fruit in the Bathsheba and Uriah affair.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-27/

- **Constable (moderate):** David was "clearing the Promised Land of foreign foes so the Israelites could occupy it," acting in accord with Deut 3:18–20 and Josh 1:13. Yet he "walked a thin line of deception" with Achish.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Notes that David was "doubtless animated therein by public spirit and religious zeal (1 Sam 30:26), but his motives were not altogether unmixed."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/27.htm

- **Matthew Henry (balancing):** "While David was in the land of the Philistines, he attacked some remains of the devoted nations. The people whom he cut off were long before doomed to destruction. It is often wisdom to shun public notice, but we must in no situation be idle. We must always try to do somewhat in the cause of God."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/27.htm

**Key difference among traditions:** The Reformed/Baptist strain (Gill, partly Henry) tends to view the raids as legitimate holy war against Canaanite remnants under the ban. The Anglican/higher-critical strain (Ellicott) and Pentecostal/charismatic (Guzik) are more willing to call David's actions sinful. Constable (Evangelical/Dispensational) takes a middle view — the targets were legitimate, but the deception was not.

---

### vv. 10–11 — David's deception of Achish

- **Gill:** David's answer was "an equivocation, and made with a design to deceive; and was by no means agreeably to the character of David, nor to be defended nor imitated." He notes Abarbinel's opinion that these tribes were also enemies of Achish, so the deception was less dangerous than it appears — but Gill himself does not endorse this.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Ellicott:** "The answer of David to his sovereign lord, the King of Gath — for he was now, to all intents and purposes, a vassal prince of Achish — was simply a falsehood." He notes that David represented the booty as captured from his own countrymen.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Pulpit Commentary on v. 11:** The A.V. rendering "to bring tidings" is wrong; the Hebrew means "to bring them [prisoners] to Gath." Prisoners were normally part of the spoil of war and would be sold as slaves. David killed them all so none could betray him. The phrase "so will be his manner all the while he dwelleth" should instead read (per the narrator): "And so was his manner all the days that he dwelt in the field of the Philistines."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/27.htm

- **Matthew Henry:** "But an equivocation which serves the purpose of a lie, is as like to it as a hypocrite is to a profane person, it is only better in appearance, therefore more dangerous."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/27.htm

- **Enduring Word:** "David didn't lie to Achish because he was ashamed of what he did. He lied to gain favor with Achish." He killed entire villages to cover his lies, planting a pattern — covering sin with murder — that would recur with Bathsheba and Uriah.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-27/

---

### v. 12 — Achish is deceived into trusting David

- **Gill:** Achish believed David because David "imposed upon him by ambiguous terms, insinuating he had been against the southern parts of Judah, when he had been against foreign nations that lay to the south of Judah." Achish reasoned that David had made himself so odious to Israel that he could never return, and would therefore remain Achish's servant forever.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

- **Enduring Word:** "Achish felt he was in a good place. David was trapped in a web and Achish was the spider… It all looked rather dark, but David had not — and could not — burn his bridge with God."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-27/

- **Constable:** Cites Miscall: "Like Nabal (in 1 Samuel 25:10), Achish seriously underestimates David by regarding him as a servant or slave."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-27.html

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** The chapter closes with a picture of David in great apparent success — security, wealth from raids, the trust of a king — but all built on a foundation of deceit and spiritual decline. "If a man will put himself among Philistines, he cannot promise to come forth innocent" (Bishop Hall, quoted in Pulpit).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/27.htm

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ

1. **The ethics of David's raids (vv. 8–9):** The sharpest divide is between those who see the total destruction of Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites as legitimate holy war (Gill/Baptist-Reformed, citing Deuteronomic ban passages) and those who see it as unjustifiable cruelty driven by expediency (Ellicott/Anglican, Guzik/Pentecostal). Constable (Evangelical) splits the difference: legitimate targets, illegitimate deception.

2. **Assessment of David's overall spiritual state:** The Reformed tradition (as represented in the *Reformation Study Bible*, quoted by Precept Austin) says David "gives in to human fear" despite recently learned lessons of faith. The Pentecostal/charismatic reading (Enduring Word) emphasises the emotional dynamics — discouragement and despair as David's real enemies — which fits that tradition's attention to the inner life and spiritual warfare. Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed) strikes a pastoral balance: "Unbelief is a sin that easily besets even good men… yet, though believers often manifest imperfections, they can never be prevailed upon to renounce the service of God."

3. **The silence of God:** All traditions note the absence of God's name and David's failure to inquire of the Lord — but they draw different implications. The Reformed reading (Pink, quoted by Precept Austin) stresses the sovereignty of God silently overruling David's folly. The Pentecostal reading (Guzik) stresses the quenching of the Spirit and the loss of David's "song."

## Other views

- **Catholic reading (Haydock's Catholic Commentary, referenced on StudyLight):** Not fully accessible in this search, but the link exists at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-samuel-27.html .

- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** Not fetched in this session, but the NET Bible is available at https://netbible.org and typically provides textual and historical-critical notes on each verse, including the ambiguous Hebrew phrasing of v. 7 ("days and four months") and v. 11.

- **Josephus** (cited by Gill): Makes David's stay "four months and twenty days" rather than a year and four months, and claims David "spared the men, and abstained from the slaughter of them, fearing lest they should declare to the king what he had done" — the opposite of what the biblical text says.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-27.html

---

## Summary

The nearly unanimous traditional reading sees chapter 27 as David's spiritual low point — a faith failure in which discouragement drives him from the promised land into a web of compromise, deception, and violence. As Precept Austin summarises, "He feared man (Saul), not God." The chapter sets up the crisis of chapters 29–30, where God in His providence both rescues David from fighting against Israel (ch. 29) and disciplines him through the Amalekite raid on Ziklag (ch. 30), leading to David's repentance and return to the Lord (1 Sam 30:6).
